summary:
TERRALYTX finds places on Earth that match the ground on the Moon and Mars, so that rovers, suits and tools can be tested where conditions really match. Today, test sites are mostly chosen by reputation.

We measured slope and roughness on NASA LRO LOLA lunar south pole terrain and the NASA Mars 2020 Jezero terrain model. Then we compared them with 1.46 million 10 km squares of Earth elevation data. Using successive Pareto fronts across slope, roughness, and terrain connectivity, we selected 400 geographically separated candidates without combining the measurements into an arbitrary match score; the closest, Volcán Aracar in Argentina, has a slope-distribution distance of 0.80° against the Connecting Ridge near Shackleton crater. We also screened geologic maps for the lake rocks Curiosity and Perseverance found, which identified the Lockatong Formation near Princeton.

Maps are only a start. Our low-cost FieldKit, an iPhone with LiDAR and a 3D-printed frame, captured 6 scans and 364 photos at Sourland Mountain. Anyone near a candidate site can add evidence. Every scan is checked automatically, and a site moves from "seen from space" to "confirmed on the ground" only when the evidence holds up.

Testing on Earth is far cheaper than mistakes on another world. TERRALYTX turns choosing an analog site into an open, measurable process that anyone can help with.
details:
What it does and how it works

TERRALYTX finds places on Earth that match the ground on the Moon and Mars. That helps teams choose where to test rovers, suits and tools on measured evidence rather than reputation.

From orbit:

We took height maps of eight Moon and Mars sites from NASA's LRO laser altimeter (LOLA) and the USGS/NASA Jezero terrain model. At each site we measured slope and roughness at four scales, from 400 m to 3.2 km. We then measured the same thing on 1.46 million 10 km land squares of Copernicus GLO-90 Earth elevation, with ESA WorldCover masking out water and ice. Rather than combining slope, roughness, and terrain connectivity into an arbitrary match score, we used successive Pareto fronts to identify candidates that performed well across all three criteria, followed by geographic separation to avoid selecting nearby duplicates. This produced 400 nominated terrain records. We report slope-distribution distance separately, using the Wasserstein-1 distance in degrees, where lower means closer. That distance is judged against a yardstick: real spots on the Moon differ from each other by 3.66°. The closest Moon match, Volcán Aracar in Argentina, has a slope-distribution distance of 0.80° against the Connecting Ridge near the lunar south pole. Of the 400 best matches, 143 are in the Andes, where analog testing already happens; TERRALYTX was never told that.

Rock maps:

We compared global (GLiM) and US (SGMC) geologic maps with what Curiosity and Perseverance found in Mars lake rocks. A unit qualifies only if every required property is recorded and nothing rules it out. The Lockatong Formation near Princeton qualifies. In a test region we held out, the Hartford basin, every pick was correct and 86% of known lake rocks were found.

On the ground:

The FieldKit pairs iPhone LiDAR and an Intel RealSense D435 on a 3D-printed frame.

On November 15th we took it to Sourland Mountain, New Jersey, and made 6 scans and 364 photos. One 90-second scan produced a 160,656-triangle mesh with a passed drift check.

Diabase ridge with boulder fields this is not an official NASA analog, which is why we measure it. Diabase is very similar to the basalt on the martian terrain.

Benefits

1) Analog sites are chosen by measured evidence, not by reputation.

2) Every one of the 600 records states its evidence level, from "seen from orbit or map" up to "corroborated."

3) Scans are checked automatically, problems are flagged rather than hidden, and nothing is smoothed or filled in.

4) The kit costs a fraction of a survey-grade setup.

Intended impact

1) Anyone can contribute. A hiker, student or local club near a candidate site can scan the ground with a phone and add real evidence.

2) It fills a known gap. A 2024 USGS survey of planetary scientists found analog field data scattered and hard to find (Open-File Report 2024-1042) and encourages independent researchers to find

3) Trust is earned. Every scan is checked automatically and labelled honestly. A site moves from "seen from space" to "confirmed on the ground" only when the evidence holds up.

4) Better test sites. Rover and suit teams get a growing, worldwide map of test sites they can rely on.

5) Space exploration from your backyard. The public gets a real way to take part in Moon and Mars missions.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

1) Python (NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib)

2) NASA LRO LOLA, the USGS/NASA Jezero DTM, Copernicus GLO-90, ESA WorldCover, GLiM, USGS SGMC, and published Curiosity and Perseverance papers

3) iPhone LiDAR, Intel RealSense D435, a MacBook

4) Autodesk Fusion for CAD

5) H2D and A1 3d printer for printing PLA, PETG and TPU 95A

6) Flutter and Dart for the mobile app and the desktop

7) React, TS, JS, HTML, CSS for the dashboard (web app)

8) AI was used as an assistant.

Creativity

1) The same slope-and-roughness measurement works from orbit and on the ground, so a field scan can directly check the orbit score.

2) The scores are honest distances, never percentages, and they are judged against real variation between Moon sites.

3) The FieldKit brings industrial-style mapping to a hobbyist budget.

Factors we considered

1) Honesty about evidence: every result is labelled built, tested or planned.

2) Limits: Antarctica is not yet covered, 138 squares failed to load, and the kit's accuracy is untested against a reference scanner.

3) Rock maps are screening only, with no mineral conclusions drawn from scans.

4) Contributor privacy: exact locations are hidden by default.

5) No hard plastic touches the computer, and the soft grips can be replaced.
